cover.artAlt: The Great Pyramids of Giza glowing golden at sunset with the Sphinx in the foreground
cover.blurb: The pyramids are glowing gold in the sunset, and the Sphinx is waiting to meet you. Turn the page and step into the amazing world of ancient Egypt!

pages.title: The Lion with a Human Face
pages.artAlt: A close-up of the Great Sphinx's stone face glowing in warm afternoon light

facts.text: The Great Sphinx was not built from blocks like a wall. Long ago, workers dug a huge horseshoe shaped quarry and carved the whole statue from one single mass of limestone rock. That makes it one of the largest and oldest statues ever carved from a single piece of stone.

The Sphinx has the body of a lion and the head of a person. Sculptors began shaping it about 4,500 years ago, in the time of the pharaoh Khafre. It has rested on its rocky plateau ever since, watching the sun rise and set over the sand.
This gentle giant is about 20 metres tall and more than 70 metres long, which is longer than half a football pitch. Even lying down, it towers over the visitors who come to say hello.

pages.title: Secrets in the Stone
pages.artAlt: Rows of hieroglyphs carved into a sandstone temple wall

facts.text: Hieroglyphs are a kind of picture writing. Each sign shows something from the real world, such as a person, an animal or a plant. The ancient Egyptians used these beautiful little pictures to write down their spoken language.

The word hieroglyph means sacred carving. Stone workers chiselled hieroglyphs into temples and monuments for nearly 3,000 years. Later on, writers also used reed pens and ink to write them on papyrus.

For hundreds of years nobody could read hieroglyphs, until soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799. It carries the same message in three different scripts, and one of them was Ancient Greek, which scholars could still read. Using that clue, Jean-Francois Champollion cracked the hieroglyphic code in 1822.

pages.title: The River Road
pages.artAlt: A traditional wooden sailboat drifts past reeds on the Nile at golden hour

facts.text: Every year the Nile rose and flooded the land beside it, leaving behind water and rich dark silt. That soft soil was perfect for growing food, so farms and villages grew up all along the riverbanks. The Egyptians even planned their whole calendar around the flood, the growing season and the harvest.

Ancient Egypt did not need many roads, because the Nile was its highway. Sailing was the easiest way to travel, and boats carried people, food and even enormous stones for building projects. Wooden sailboats still glide along the river today, just like the one in this picture.

Astronauts looking down from space can spot the Nile easily. Its dark green ribbon of fields and trees stands out sharply against the light tan desert all around. At night the valley glows too, because so many towns light up along the water.

pages.title: A Face of Gold
pages.artAlt: A golden pharaoh's mask shines softly in a museum display

facts.text: Ancient goldsmiths made this mask by heating and hammering sheets of gold until they joined together. The eyes are made of shiny obsidian and quartz, and the eyebrows are inlaid with a deep blue stone called lapis lazuli. Around the shoulders, a broad collar sparkles with coloured glass and precious stones.

In 1922, an archaeologist named Howard Carter peered into a hidden room that had been closed for thousands of years. When someone asked if he could see anything, he answered, yes, wonderful things. Inside were more than 5,000 objects belonging to the young king Tutankhamun.

Today the golden mask has a shiny new home at the Grand Egyptian Museum, near the pyramids of Giza. There it joins thousands of other treasures from Tutankhamun, displayed together for the first time. Every one of them helps us discover how clever and creative ancient Egyptian makers really were.
